figures.caption: Figure 1: Mothers’ and fathers’ childcare time in South Korea. Source: H. Park (2021) using Korean Time Use Survey (KTUS) estimates for married parents with at least one child under school age.

Figure 2: Total fertility rates and average years of schooling in South Korea. Panel (a) covers the period 1960–2024 and uses data from the World Bank annual series through 2023 and 2024 official birth statistics from Statistics Korea. Panel (b) relies on Barro-Lee Educational Attainment Data.

Figure 8: Comparing equilibrium points of human capital and population size. Parameters A = 3.75, β = 0.5, γ = 0.5, ϕ = 0.0025, b = 0.1. In the perfect complements case, k̄ is 12.83 and N̄ is 50.95, close to Korea’s current levels, 12 and 51.6, respectively.
Figure 4: Comparing equilibria when dad and mom’s time allocated to parenting are perfect substitutes vs complements. Parameters A = 3.75, α = 0.1, β = 0.5, γ = 0.5, ϕ = 0.0025.

Figure 3: Main elements of the model. The parental-care technology determines whether maternal and paternal time are perfect substitutes or perfect complements, which in turn shapes fertility, education, and the steady-state comparison.
Figure 5: A comparison of intra-household time allocation and the corresponding output implications.
Figure 6: Comparing equilibria for different education returns. Parameters A = 3.75, β = 0.5, γ = 0.5, ϕ = 0.0025.
Figure 7: Comparing equilibria for different education returns. Parameters A = 3.75, β = 0.5, γ = 0.5, ϕ = 0.0025.
